text.hook:
Data race. Race condition. Deadlock.
Three different bugs that get mixed up in interviews all the time.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Three failures, three layers
2. The exact definition of a data race
3. Why ++counter loses updates
4. Coffman's four conditions, and how to break them
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: two threads write two different `int` members of the same struct, no lock. Data race or not? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No: different members are different memory locations (it may still cause false sharing). Adjacent bit-fields are different: they form one memory location, so that is a data race.

slides.lead: Three different bugs. The mental model to tell them apart, plus 6 myths.

slides.title: Three failures, three different layers

cards.label: Data race
cards.text: A language rule broken: unsynchronized conflicting access. UB for the whole program.

cards.label: Race condition
cards.text: A logic bug: correct only for some interleavings. Possible with zero data races.

cards.label: Deadlock
cards.text: A progress failure: threads wait on each other in a cycle, forever.

slides.takeaway: Answer at the C++ level first. Hardware stories are just one possible execution.

slides.title: All four, at the same time
items: Same memory location, at least one write (they *conflict*)
At least one access is not atomic
slides.warn: Result: undefined behaviour for the entire program, not "a slightly wrong value".

slides.title: Why `++counter` is not atomic
slides.takeaway: Even x86 `add [mem], 1` without `lock` is load, add, store. The compiler may also keep `counter` in a register.

slides.lead: `x = 10` vs `x = 20` under one mutex: no data race, final value 10 or 20. A mutex never decides who goes first.

slides.title: Coffman: all four must hold. Break one.
rows: lock-free or immutable data, single owner
slides.takeaway: "No preemption" is about resources. The OS preempting a thread never releases its mutex.

slides.title: Rules that keep you deadlock-free
items: Impose one global lock order (not creation order)
Never call unknown code (callbacks, virtuals) while holding a lock
Never block on another thread (`join`, `future.get()`) while holding a lock
slides.warn: Timeouts (`try_lock_for`) are diagnostics and escape hatches, not prevention.

items.myth: "I joined both threads, so it is safe."
items.truth: `join()` orders each worker before the code after it. It does not protect the workers from each other.

items.myth: "x86 is cache coherent, so a plain shared `int` is fine."
items.truth: C++ rules and the compiler apply first. Coherence does not make RMW atomic or stop hoisting.

items.myth: "A read racing with a write just reads a stale value."
items.truth: It is UB: torn values, hoisted loads and deleted loops are all real outcomes.

items.myth: "If every variable is atomic, my class is thread-safe."
items.truth: Multi-step invariants still need one critical section or one RMW.

items.myth: "`lock_guard` notices a deadlock and backs off."
items.truth: RAII wrappers just call `lock()`. They detect nothing.

items.myth: "TSan finds data races, but not deadlocks."
items.truth: TSan also reports lock-order inversions. For a live hang, use a debugger.

slides.hero:
Data race:
undefined program.

Race condition:
wrong program.

Deadlock:
stuck program.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Two threads. One mutex. 100000 locked increments each. 🔒

The author expects 200000. What does it actually print?
Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: This exact bug shows up in code reviews and interviews. The compiler even warns about it, and people still miss it.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: braces fixed, but each thread locks a different mutex. What prints now? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Still a data race, so undefined behaviour: two different mutexes give no mutual exclusion between the threads. In practice the result is usually less than 200000.

slides.title:
The author expects 200000.
What is printed?

slides.verdict_sub: and it is a data race (undefined behaviour)
bullets: No braces: the loop body is **only** the `lock_guard` declaration.
The guard locks and unlocks 100000 times, protecting nothing.
`++counter` runs once per thread, **after** the loop, unlocked.

slides.tip: GCC warns with `-Wall` (-Wmisleading-indentation). Treat warnings as errors in concurrent code.
slides.takeaway: A lock protects exactly the scope of its guard object. Always check where that scope ends.

text.hook:
"Data race" and "race condition" are not synonyms.
Can you explain the difference in one sentence?

Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜ for the answer.
text.body: A classic opener in C++ concurrency interviews. The precise answer is short.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: does marking a shared `bool` flag `volatile` fix a data race on it? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. volatile is not a synchronization primitive in C++: it gives no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering. Use std::atomic<bool>.

slides.title: What is the difference between a data race and a race condition?
options: Data race: unsynchronized conflicting access, UB. Race condition: logic that depends on timing.
None. A data race is just one kind of race condition.
Make every shared variable `std::atomic` and both are gone.
A data race only matters on weakly ordered CPUs like ARM.

slides.verdict_sub: Data race = undefined program. Race condition = wrong program.
bullets: Data race: a property of memory accesses. TSan can catch it.
Race condition: a property of the algorithm. Every access may be legal.
Race condition, no data race: `if (stock.load() > 0) stock.fetch_sub(1);`
Data race, no race condition: two threads store `true` to a plain `bool done`. Still UB.
slides.cta: Why not B, C or D ➜

items: B: a data race can exist where the logic does not depend on order at all. It is a language rule, not a logic bug.
C: atomics remove data races, not check-then-act races.
D: a data race is UB by the C++ rules on any hardware. The compiler relies on it.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "Data-race-free is the minimum bar for a defined program. Race-condition-free is the bar for a correct one."

text.hook:
Only one mutex in the whole program.
So a deadlock is impossible. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The usual suspect is two mutexes locked in opposite order. This one hides somewhere else.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: on failure to lock the second mutex, release the first and retry. Deadlock is gone. What new problem can appear? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Livelock: two threads with symmetric timing can lock, fail, release and retry in lockstep forever at 100% CPU. Add randomized back-off or keep one consistent lock order.

slides.title: One mutex. Can this deadlock?

bullets: `main` owns `m` (`g` lives until the end of `main`), then waits in `join()`.
The worker blocks in `lock()` on `m`, so it can never finish.
Circular wait with one mutex: the second "resource" is *the worker has finished*.

slides.title: Never join while holding a lock
slides.tip: Same shape: `future.get()` or waiting on a full queue while holding a lock the other thread needs.
slides.takeaway: A deadlock needs a cycle of waits, not two mutexes.

text.hook:
"Every member is std::atomic, so the class is thread-safe."

True or false?
Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜ for the answer.
text.body: A favourite design question. The answer is about invariants, not variables.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up an interviewer would ask next: "notify() holds the class's std::mutex while it calls subscriber callbacks. One callback calls subscribe(), which locks the same mutex. What happens?" Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: The same thread locks a std::mutex it already owns: undefined behaviour, in practice a self-deadlock. Copy the subscriber list under the lock, release it, then call out.

slides.title: You make every member of a class `std::atomic`. Is the class now thread-safe?
options: Yes: atomics make every access safe.
Yes, if you use acquire/release instead of relaxed.
Not necessarily: multi-step invariants can still break.
No: atomics still race under heavy contention.

slides.verdict_sub: Data-race-free, but invariants can still break
bullets: Two threads both read 103, both decide 104 is next.
Both apply message 104: duplicate processing, **zero** data races.
Fix: one critical section for check + apply + publish, or one owner thread.
slides.cta: Why not A, B or D ➜

items: A: each atomic operation is indivisible. A check followed by an act is two operations.
B: memory ordering controls visibility, not the logic of a multi-step algorithm.
D: operations on the same atomic object are never a data race, under any contention.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "Thread safety is about invariants, not individual variables. Single-owner state plus queues often beats sprinkling atomics."

text.hook:
std::scoped_lock is deadlock-free.
So a self-transfer is harmless... right? ⚠️

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: One aliasing case that "deadlock-free" code forgets. Self-transfers, self-swaps and self-merges all hit it.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: how can a debug build turn a lock-order violation into an immediate error instead of a rare production hang? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: A hierarchical mutex: each mutex gets a level, a thread_local remembers the level this thread currently holds, and locking a mutex whose level is not lower throws.

slides.title:
scoped_lock, self-transfer.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: libstdc++: prints `start`, then spins at 100% CPU forever
bullets: The same `std::mutex` is passed twice: `std::lock(m, m)`.
It locks `m`, then calls `try_lock` on `m`, which it already owns: UB.
libstdc++: `try_lock` fails, it unlocks and retries forever. A one-thread livelock.
Deadlock avoidance only works for **distinct** mutexes.

slides.title: Handle aliasing before you lock
slides.tip: Aliasing is common: self-transfers, swapping an object with itself, merging a container into itself.
slides.takeaway: Always handle aliasing before multi-locking. Now it prints `done 100`.
